newsitem.title: USA: ATHLETICS-SUSPENDED HURDLER FLENOY COMPETES, BUT IS LAST.
newsitem.headline: ATHLETICS-SUSPENDED HURDLER FLENOY COMPETES, BUT IS LAST.

text.p: Suspended 400-meter hurdler Stephon Flenoy got his chance to run in the U.S. athletics championships on Friday but finished last in his preliminary race.
Flenoy's complicated situation came to a head Friday when the IAAF waived its "contamination" rule, which could have led to the suspension of all runners who competed against him.

Even with the IAAF backing away from its hardline stance, the race went off only after the competitors, including world record-holder Kevin Young, signed a waiver form from U.S. track officials conceding that they knew about the contamination risk.
The rule by the sport's international governing body states that athletes can be suspended if they knowingly compete against ineligible athletes.

"I applaud the other athletes for their courage to sign the waiver to allow me to compete," said the little-known hurdler who had won an arbitrator's hearing on Wednesday that reinstated him into the championships.
"That was my intention from the start, to fight for the right to compete here, and (for) any others down the road who find themselves in this situation."
Flenoy had been suspended by the USA Track and Field (USATF) April 4, after a drug test revealed a ratio of testosterone to epitestosterone higher than the acceptable 6-to-1.
He took the case to arbitration and an aribtrator ruled that he had not received a fair hearing before a USATF board and ordered him reinstated into the U.S. championships.
Although under U.S. law the arbitrator's ruling was binding on USA Track and Field, the IAAF, as late as Friday, had threatened to invoke the contamination rule.

But IAAF secretary general Istvan Gyulai said a majority IAAF Council in a telephone vote "exceptionally agreed to waive the rule" with one condition: that Flenoy's result be void and that he not be allowed to compete in the world championships if he made the team.
The latter stipulation was never in question as the 29-year-old Flenoy trailed badly from the start and finished last in his race.
The IAAF decision came after a letter from USATF president Pat Rico to IAAF president Primo Nebiolo requested the waiver on behalf of 400-meter hurdlers in the championships.
"The athletes expressed full commitment to IAAF rules," Gyulai said in a telephone interview from Monoco.
Gyulai said the athletes had grave concerns about their eligibility and were "considering withdrawing from the competition."

He added that the hurdlers were aware Flenoy's suspension under IAAF rules could not be lifted by a U.S. arbitration panel and that the waiver was granted only after the IAAF tried unsuccessfully to prevent Flenoy from competing.
